### 5.1.2.9 Executive summary
FNB Insurance Brokers and FNB Life currently offer a view of both Short-
Term and Life Insurance products to active Online Banking Customers via FNB Online and FNB App. T
### he Insurance Tab, once selected has two sub tabs which provide a summary and detailed view of all S
### hort Term and
FNB Life products the customer may have with FNB, with additional Policy and Claim assistance reque
sts.
The recent amalgamation of FNB Life & the Life Insurance Team, [from now on referred to as FNB Life I
nsurance] has caused a shift in thinking around the broader insurance business and strategy with a vie
w to “Build for the Future”. With this in mind, existing products offered by the Life business are being re
### vised in order to standardize and introduce new product offerings under the FirstRand Life License. Th
e intent is to sell, administer and run claims for a comprehensive range of integrated insurance produc
ts on the new Policy Administration System.
As a result, the FNB-
APP Insurance Tab offerings need to allow for the new thinking which includes but not limited to:-
Providing a consolidated view of all Insurance Products the customer holds
Enabling self service functionality for Life Insurance products
Providing a detailed view of customer and policy information and
Creating and executing an effective sales strategy
### 5.1.2.10 Background and context
Purpose
The purpose of this document is to outline the technical design for the solution, including the technolo
gy and infrastructure, system integration, and configuration options for maintenance and support. The
document also provides a basis for building other applications to consume the
ALIS_ESB web service.
Intended Audience
The intended audience of this document are OCEP developers, architecture team, and FNB Life develo
pers.

Design Goals
The following design goals were taken into account:
FNB Life OCEP Platform to be developed based on industry best practices, including the use of r
ecommended naming conventions, OOP design methodology and design patterns.
Code to be clear with sufficient comments and documentation;
FNB Life OCEP Platform must be easily maintainable and configurable without requiring code ch
anges for some parts of the system;
Assumption and constraints
The following assumptions and constraints have been made in regards to the design, support and enh
ancements of the OCEP platform - FNB Life:
ALIS-ESB must be accessible at all times to ensure the users have uninterrupted service
OCEP framework environment is available and running when the tab is accessed

Dynatrace uses patented PurePath Technology to capture timing and code-level context for every
transaction, across every tier, without gaps or blind spots.
Drill into all services and components called upon with each user interaction.
Analyze response times and find hotspots at the method level.
Understand the impact of methods and database statements on user experience using our
unique Service backtrace feature.

### 5.1.3.8 Executive summary
This document describes the event information that can be populated when making calls to the OCEP
frameworks. These events are used by Google Marketing Platform (GMP) to track progress of
applications and other user interactions.
Background and context
Purpose
The purpose of this document is to outline the technical design for the solution, including the technolo
gy and infrastructure, system integration, and configuration options for maintenance and support.
In order to maximise the impact of digital marketing campaigns, all activity needs to be tracked via
Google Tag Manager Floodlights & Firebase events so as to enable the capability of real time reporting
and optimisation of campaigns.
Current tracking is in place for all Appazon sales processes on [FNB.co.za](http://FNB.co.za)33, FNB.mobi and App
through product specific floodlights & Firebase tracking as well as call me back tracking. The
requirement is to expand to also include FNB Life Insurance processes now.
Intended Audience
The intended audience of this document are OCEP developers, architecture team, and FNB Life develo
pers.
Design Goals
The following design goals were taken into account:
Product specific events on Firebase for all New Life product sales processes on FNB App
Insurance tab.
FNB Life OCEP Firebase events must be easily maintainable and configurable without requiring
major code changes for new events i the future;

## 6 FNB Life OCEP - System Development
## 6.1 Development process
This picture shows high level software development process
The following things must be taken into consideration when one is doing software development:
### 1. A developer needs to attend business requirements specification (BRS) walk-through so that he\she
understands what is required as an end product of development.
1. Functional requirements specification (FRS) should be a guide for a developer to start his\her
## system design
1. Technical design document together with FRS should help a developer when he\she starts with
implementation phase.
- Use case diagram
- System Flowcharts
- Domain objects (Entity diagram can be used for this if there's database design involved)
- Class diagram which all classes involved in the solution
- Sequence diagram to show interaction between objects
1. Coding best practices must be followed, e.g. if a language being used is Java, developer must
follow Java coding standards
1. Use design patterns like MVC (where applicable) to make sure that systems are scalable. Singleton,
Factory and AbstractFactory patterns are some of the common design patterns
FNB Life OCEP - System Development – 54

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
1. Developer must make sure that they are using version control system like SVN, CVS, etc. There
needs to be a structure in SVN to support project versioning, production code rollback and new
projects. This is realized by using Branches, Trunk, and Tags on SVN.
1. unit testing must be performed before code is released to QA
1. Use code optimization tools available on your IDE to refactor code.
6.2 Life Insurance Digital Dev Coding standards
6.2.1 OCEP
Description:
A Java coding standards template is important to ensure consistency, readability, and maintainability
across a software project. Below we are covering key aspects like naming conventions, formatting,
and best practices.
6.2.1.1 1. Naming Conventions
6.2.1.1.1 1.1 Classes and Interfaces
Classes: Use PascalCase (UpperCamelCase).
Example: CustomerService , OrderManager
Interfaces: Use PascalCase with adjectives or nouns that describe capabilities.
Example: Runnable , Serializable
6.2.1.1.2 1.2 Methods
```
Methods: Use camelCase.
```
Example: getCustomerDetails() , processOrder()
6.2.1.1.3 1.3 Variables
Local Variables: Use camelCase.
Example: customerName , orderList
Constants: Use UPPERCASE with underscores separating words.
Example: MAX_RETRY_COUNT , DEFAULT_TIMEOUT
FNB Life OCEP - System Development – 55

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
##### 6.2.1.1.4 1.4 Packages
Package Names: Use all lowercase, with domain structure.
Example: com.companyname.project.module
##### 6.2.1.1.5 1.5 Enums
Enum Names: Use PascalCase.
Example: OrderStatus
Enum Constants: Use UPPERCASE.
Example: PENDING , COMPLETED
##### 6.2.1.2 2. Formatting
##### 6.2.1.2.1 2.1 Indentation
Use 4 spaces per indentation level. Never use tabs.
##### 6.2.1.2.2 2.2 Line Length
Limit line length to 500 characters. If exceeding, break lines appropriately.
##### 6.2.1.2.3 2.3 Braces
Always use braces {} for if, else, for, while, and do statements, even if optional.
Opening braces should be on the same line as the statement.
##### 6.2.1.2.4 2.4 Blank Lines
Use blank lines to separate logical code blocks for readability.
Example
FNB Life OCEP - System Development – 56

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
### 6.2.1.3 3. Commenting and Documentation
### 6.2.1.3.1 3.1 Javadoc
All public classes and methods should include Javadoc comments.
### 6.2.1.3.2 3.2 Inline Comments
Use inline comments sparingly and only when necessary to explain complex logic.
### 6.2.1.4 4. Code Structure
### 6.2.1.4.1 4.1 Order of Members
The following order should be used for class members:
FNB Life OCEP - System Development – 57

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
1. Constants: (public, private, or protected)
1. Fields: (private, protected, public)
1. Constructors
1. Methods: (public, protected, private)
1. Inner Classes: (if any)
##### 6.2.1.4.2 4.2 Method Length
Keep methods short and focused on a single task. A method should ideally not exceed 40 lines.
##### 6.2.1.4.3 4.3 Exception Handling
Always catch specific exceptions instead of generic Exception
##### 6.2.1.4.4 4.4 Logging
###### Use a standard logging framework (e.g., Log4j, SLF4J) for logging errors and info.
##### 6.2.1.5 5. Best Practices
##### 6.2.1.5.1 5.1 Avoid Magic Numbers
###### Define meaningful constants for any hardcoded numbers
FNB Life OCEP - System Development – 58

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
##### 6.2.1.5.2 5.2 Use Final Keyword Where Appropriate
##### Use final for variables that should not be reassigned
##### 6.2.1.5.3 5.3 Avoid Code Duplication
Reuse code via methods or utility classes instead of duplicating logic.
##### 6.2.1.5.4 5.4 Optimize Imports
##### Do not use wildcard imports. Only import specific classes
##### 6.2.1.5.5 5.5 Use Streams and Lambdas Carefully
##### While lambdas and streams enhance readability, avoid overly complex stream operations that
##### reduce code clarity.

standalone/configuration)

</system-properties>

already by other applications, else change it to 8081

##### 6.3.2.2.2 Insurance Image Naming Convention
Important to note:
All insurance images must have the prefix: resource.life.
###### There must be five Android images with these suffixes: .hdpi, .mdpi, .xhdpi, .xxhdpi, .xxxhdpi
###### There must be two iOS images with these suffixes: @2x, @3x
###### There must be two Mobi images with these suffixes: .mdpi, .ldpi
File format/extension for insurance images must be: .png
Example of an iOS resource:
resource.life.example@2x.png
resource.life.example@3x.png
Example of an android resource:
resource.life.example.hdpi.png
resource.life.example.mdpi.png
resource.life.example.xhdpi.png
resource.life.example.xxhdpi.png
resource.life.example.xxxhdpi.png

copying them from the INT server to QA while maintaining the same directory structure.

f
### Monthly Deals:
File name is monthly.deals.pdf
FNB Life OCEP - System Development – 71

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
This file is updated monthly to reflect wellness offers specific to that month.
An MFT process is used to update the prod pdf on a monthly basis.
Wellness Offers:
File name is WellnessOffers.json
This file holds all the content being displayed by the Wellness Offers screens.
Dischem Stores:
File name is dischem_final_locations.csv
This file contains information such as store name, store location, and coordinates of the
Dischem stores users can send their script orders to.
MFT processes have been set up to automate the updating of this file whenever Dischem adds
new stores or updates existing ones.
Credit Card Ts and Cs:
File names are FNB_CreditCard_MedicalBenefitTsCs_2020.pdf
and RMB_CreditCard_MedicalBenefitTsCs_2020.pdf
These files contains terms and conditions for FNB and RMB Credit Card medical spend offers.
##### 6.3.3.3.3 Monthly Deals MFT Process
High level monthly deals production process is as below:
monthly.deals.pdf > \\10.33.130.174\mft\OCEP\Outbound > PROD Node 1 and Node 2 in directory "/
opt/wildfly/releases/files/"

### 6.7 OCEP Resources
### 6.7.1 OCEP
Description:
Omni Channel Enablement Platform (OCEP) is a Digital banking initiative and framework that is used
internal to digital banking to enable the development of business functionality in a simple common
framework that has the ability to expose presentation layer flows and functionality to Online Banking,
Phone App and Tablet App.
Below is a list of resources an OCEP developer will need to develop and test on the OCEP platform.

### 6.8 Performance (Online and App service calls)
### 6.8.1 Steps:
1. Run the below script in the directory with your log files:
grep -e " build_your_own_" -e "call took" -e "StartUWApplication Response Time:" -e "List
Accounts Response" OnlineApplication.log | grep -v Overview | grep -v "build_your_own_6" | sed
-e "s/ms.//g" | sed -e "s/ms//g" | awk '{a[NR]=$0} END{for(i=1;i<=NR;i++) if(a[i+1]!~/List
Accounts/) print a[i]}' | awk '{ if ($10 == "build_your_own_1" || $10 == "build_your_own_2" || $10 ==
"build_your_own_3" || $10 == "build_your_own_underwriting" || $10 == "build_your_own_5" || $10
== "build_your_own_7") print " " $2 "," $10 ","$13","; else if ($7 == "StartUWApplication") printf
",,"$7","$10","; else if ($7 == "List") printf ",,,,,,"$7$8","$11","; else printf $10","$13","; fi;}' | sed -e "s/
TIME://g" | sed -e "s/- //g" | awk '{ f=$1; l=$NF; $1=l; $NF=f; print}' | sed -e "s/ //g" > Online.txt
a. grep all key words that record response times e.g. build_your_own_1 Response Time: 17425ms
### (total response of byo1 page)
b. grep -v, pages to be excluded from the report e.g. (grep -v "build_your_own_6")
c. remove ms from the times, we only want the digit value e.g. (sed -e "s/ms.//g")
d. print the page and times (awk)
e. Output in the file Online.txt is csv lines
e.g. 09:15:04,536,build_your_own_underwriting,10368,MaintainProposal,4031,,,StartUWApplication,6271,
f. We paste in excel and do data to column on comma separation
Final presentation

### 6.9 Software development process
1. A key feature of the design process is to attempt to isolate the various ‘layers’ that make up the
overall architecture to ensure that changes in one layer have a minimal effect upon other layers in the
### system, such as for example in the business layer.
1. In following an OOD-based approach it is vital that the design process is able to discriminate
between ‘objects’ and ‘classes’. An ‘object’ is a specific instance, containing a set of data and the
methods to process the data. A ‘class’ is a generalised description of a group of objects that have the
### same data item(s) and method organisation.
1. In designing objects there are four important ‘cardinal points’ to be remembered. These are:
### a. attributes – what the object knows
b. methods – what the object does
### c. states – the changes that occur due to process flow
### d. events – responses to the outside world.
1. Object definitions should be annotated with these items. This will provide the beginnings of a
### detailed specification document. In addition, each object should be put into a UML diagram set, as this
helps summarise the information into small, tight representations of each object in a standard format
– there are nine UML diagrams. In the course of the process the diagrams will be transformed into a
### class diagram that represents the relationship between the objects – in effect a blueprint for the
### structure of the business objects.
The below diagrams are necessary on the development phase, use these as examples:
FNB Life OCEP - System Development – 96

###### FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
###### FNB Life OCEP - System Development – 97

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
1. One area where careful attention to design can reap rewards in the longer term is in the interface
between the client and the so-called presentation layer. From its earliest inception in projects using the
Java language the Model View Controller (MVC) paradigm has been one of the most implemented
solutions in client-server computing. In implementations based on web technologies, such as
JavaServer Pages (JSP) there is much to be gained from separating out elements of the application
server architecture. One approach to this is given in an implementation of the MVC paradigm using
Servlets or JavaServer Pages.
For example, a Servlet (a Java class that operates on the server side to generate output in response to
a client request) could be viewed as a ‘controller’ that is responsible for processing the request from
the client – we may assume this request arrives in HTTP or HTTP (S) format. The ‘model’ is the
representation of the data stored in the database or persistence store and the ‘view’ is the code that
decides what to display next in response to the output from the controller. This is described here to
encourage developers to look at the MVC paradigm as an example of a way to break out the
components of the client-server architecture into building blocks that can be easily modified and
maintained, and gain the benefits from an OOD-based approach to the design of the system.

### 6.12 SVN Repository Structure
### 6.12.1 Overview
You must have Subversion repository that uses the standard trunk/branches/tags structure.
[Trunk](http://svnbook.red-bean.com/en/1.8/svn.tour.importing.html#svn.tour.importing.layout)81would be the main body of development, originating from the start of the project until the
### present.
[Branch](http://svnbook.red-bean.com/en/1.8/svn.branchmerge.whatis.html)82will be a copy of code derived from a certain point in the trunk that is used for applying
major changes to the code while preserving the integrity of the code in the trunk. If the major
### changes work according to plan, they are usually merged back into the trunk.
[Tag](http://svnbook.red-bean.com/en/1.8/svn.branchmerge.tags.html)83will be a point in time on the trunk or a branch that you wish to preserve. The two main
### reasons for preservation would be that either this is a major release of the software, whether
alpha, beta, RC or RTM, or this is the most stable point of the software before major revisions on
### the trunk were applied.
Checked out a local working copy of trunk. When you want to work on a new branch you’ll follow these
general steps.
Create a new branch and switch to it
Develop in your branch, periodically merging the latest changes from trunk into your branch
When your development is complete, merge changes from your branch back into trunk
[Tag](http://svnbook.red-bean.com/en/1.8/svn.branchmerge.tags.html)s

### 6.12.2 Create a new Branch
Switch your local copy to trunk (if it’s not already trunk). And again, make sure you have no local
### changes.
Next select Team > Branch/Tag… and specify [http://lfe-r3svn01.inb.co.za/svn/FnbLife/fnblife-ocep](http://lfe-r3svn01.inb.co.za/svn/FnbLife/fnblife-ocep)/
branches/yourbranch84in the Copy to URL field. This will create a branch named yourbranch.
Click Next and leave HEAD revision selected. Click Next again, enter a commit message like “Created
### the yourbranch branch”, check the “Switch working copy to new branch/tag” checkbox, and click
Finish.
That’s it! You’ve created your new branch in the repository and switched your working copy to it. Now
you can implement your major new features in your branch and commit them to subversion without
### affecting trunk.
### 6.12.3 Merge Trunk into a Branch
While you’re working on your branch, you should periodically merge the latest version of trunk into your
branch to make sure you’re not straying too far away. Eventually, you’ll also need to do this as the last
step before merging your branch back into trunk, to ensure you won’t cause any conflicts with trunk.
First you’ll need to switch your working copy to your branch, if necessary. Subversion will merge the
### changes from trunk into your working copy, and then you’ll commit your working copy to your branch
### to fully integrate the changes from trunk. So it’s vital that you start with your working copy as a mirror
of your branch. And again, ensure you have no local changes.
Click Team > Merge… and select the “Merge a range of revisions” option. Make sure “Perform pre-
merge best practices” is checked and click Next. On the next page, if it asks you to perform any
### actions, like updating your working copy, perform them and click Next.
On the next page, make sure you’re merging from trunk and getting all eligible revisions, and click
Next. Leave all of the defaults for conflict handling and click Finish.
After the merge, the results screen will show you what happened. If you got any conflicts just resolve
### them as usual. Then commit any changes to your branch, and you’re done!
### 6.12.4 Merge a Branch into Trunk
When you’ve finished development in your branch, you need to merge your branch changes back into
### trunk, so everyone else can share in the new feature you developed.
### Make sure you only perform this merge when you are completely finished with your branch! After
merging your branch into trunk, you will no longer be able to use your branch.
First, merge trunk into your branch and commit any changes to your branch, as described in the
previous section. We need to make sure your branch is consistent with trunk before merging it back.
Next, switch your working copy to trunk. Remember that Subversion merges changes into your
### working copy first, and then you commit them back to the repository. So Subversion will apply your
branch changes to your working copy of trunk, and then you commit those changes to trunk.

On the next page, make sure you’re merging from your branch and getting all eligible revisions, and

After the merge, the results screen will show you what happened. If you got any conflicts just resolve

## 7.1 SSL
Client/Server SSL setup
This is where we generate public/private keys and certificates for ssl communication
### Step 1: Generate public/private key pairs and certificates of the server, run this on command line
keytool -genkey -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 360 -alias ocepAlisKey -keystore
ocepKeyStore.jks
## If you need to add Subject Alternative Name in your certificate, use the below command:
keytool -genkeypair -keystore ocepIntKeyStore.jks -dname "CN=yourserverip, OU=FNBLIFE,
O=FNB, L=T, ST=On, C=ZA" -keypass password -storepass password -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048
-validity 360 -alias ocepIntKeyStore -ext SAN=ip:yourserverip
### Step 2: Export server certificate that must be trusted by the client and add it to trustStore file, give this
file to the client to trust.
Export certificate, run this on command line
keytool -export -alias ocepAlisKey -keystore ocepKeyStore.jks -file client.crt
## Import exported certificate to a trustStore, run this on command line
keytool -import -file client.crt -alias ocepAlisKey -keystore ocepTrustStore.jks

### 7.3.2 Pre-Upgrade Preparation
### 7.3.2.1 Key Changes from Wildfly 16 to Wildfly 21:
Java EE to Jakarta EE - Starting from Wildfly 17 a push towards adopting the new Jakarta EE
### namespace has taken place (e.g 'javax.' to 'Jakarta.'). This forms part of a broader migration
### across many Java EE technologies
Performance and stability
New features (e.g. Jakarta EE 9 and 10)
### Updated modules and dependencies
Support for newer Java versions
Security Enhancements
### 7.3.3 Backup Procedure:
In the folder /opt/wildfly folder you will find a folder named 'wildfly-16.0.0.Final' for all environments
(INT, QA, STRESS, PROD). This will serve as our backup. Do not modify or ZIP this folder because if we
### need to revert back to wildfly 16 this will be the folder we will revert back to.
### 7.3.4 New Environment Setup
### 7.3.4.1 Downloading and installing Wildfly 21
### 1. Download Wildfly 21 for Linux to your local machine from: [Wildfly 21.0.2](https://download.jboss.org/wildfly/21.0.2.Final/wildfly-21.0.2.Final.tar.gz)85
### 2. Use MFT or MobaXterm to upload [Wildfly 21.0.2](https://download.jboss.org/wildfly/21.0.2.Final/wildfly-21.0.2.Final.tar.gz) to your chosen environment (INT, QA, STRESS,
PROD). This can be done by logging into your chosen environment with your F-Number and
uploading the file to /opt/tmp folder.
### 3. Once the file is on the '/opt/tmp' folder. Switch to the Wildfly user using the following command:
'sudo su - wildfly'
### 4. Next make a new folder in /opt/wildfly and call it "wildfly-21.0.2.Final". You can do this with the
'mkdir' command. This will be the home of our new Wildfly 21 Server.
1. Extract Wildfly from the '/opt/tmp' folder into our destination folder '/opt/wildfly/
wildfly-21.0.2.Final' by using the command 'tar -xzvf /opt/tmp/wildfly-21.0.2.Final.tar.gz -C /opt/
wildfly/wildfly-21.0.2.Final --strip-components=1'
### a. The folder structure should be as follows for '/opt/wildfly/wildfly-21.0.2.Final'

##### 8.16.6.2.4
Installation Instructions
##### 1. Stop the application server ( 172.18.189.143 (see page 818) & 172.18.189.144 (see page 818) )
##### 2. Copy images folder(opt/wildfly/releases/images) from QA(172.18.189.38) to Production nodes
(172.18.189.143 (see page 818) & 172.18.189.144 (see page 818))
##### 3. Copy the WellnessOffers file /opt/wildfly/releases/files/WellnessOffers.json on
QA(172.18.189.138) to /opt/wildfly/releases/files on nodes (172.18.189.143 (see page
##### 818) & 172.18.189.144 (see page 818))
##### 4. Update the standalone.xml (/opt/wildfly/wildfly-11.0.0.Final/standalone/configuration/
standalone.xml) by updating the "wellness.staff.pilot.switched" property value under the
<system-properties> tag from true to false on nodes (172.18.189.143 (see page
##### 818) & 172.18.189.144 (see page 818)):
<property name="wellness.staff.pilot.switched" value="false"/>
1. Update the standalone.xml (/opt/wildfly/wildfly-11.0.0.Final/standalone/configuration/
standalone.xml) by adding the "wellness.excluded.questionnaire.categories" property value
under the <system-properties> tag:
<property name="wellness.excluded.questionnaire.categories" value="2,4"/>
##### 6. Build the navwellness from the repository https://git.fnb.co.za/fnb-insurance/fnb-life-ocep/
wellness/nav-wellness using the tag TAG_PROD_OCTOBER_3_2019
1. Get the latest build number from step 6 and deploy the artifact using the ocep_wellness.sh
script found on path /opt/wildfly/releases. Do these on both the production nodes
##### 8. Confirm that the navwellness.war file is deployed and other artifacts are deployed.
1. Start up the application server nodes ( 172.18.189.143 (see page 818) & 172.18.189.144 (see page
##### 818) )

## 10 OCEP - Feature Flagging Plan 2021
## 1. Background
## a) On APP it is required that on the FNB Life Insurance( OCEP APP and OCEP Online), certain
features be hidden, enabled or disabled during runtime.
b) FNB Insurance APP and Online has already implemented a feature toggle that switches on/off
certain features for all users. The current feature flagging uses the java Togglz - Core
Framework. This was rolled out to Online in 2018 and on APP in 2019.
c) Below is a plan on how we hope to review the current solution and find ways to enhance it for
future flagging of features. We may need a generic solution which other applications like
Wellness can reuse for its own feature flagging. We also need to understand other business
cases for feature flagging
Analysis, Architecting and Onboarding : June - July 2020

## 17.1 Docker and Kubernetes
## 17.1.1 Installation
### Docker Desktop is an easy-to-install application for your [Mac](https://docs.docker.com/docker-for-mac/install/) or [Windows](https://docs.docker.com/docker-for-windows/install/) environment that enables
you to start coding and containerizing in minutes. Docker Desktop includes everything you need to
### build, run, and share containerized applications right from your machine.
Follow the instructions appropriate for your operating system to download and install Docker Desktop.
## 1. [Mac](https://docs.docker.com/docker-for-mac/install/)1028
1. [Windows](https://docs.docker.com/docker-for-windows/install/)1029
1. Linux users should know this, if not read more [here](https://docs.docker.com/engine/)1030.
## 17.1.2 Docker Architecture
### Docker includes a client (Docker CLI) and server (Docker daemon) that runs on your server/pc.
### Administrators can communicate by using simple Docker CLI commands that will then talk to the
### daemon that does all the "heavy lifting" w.r.t. running, building, distributing your docker containers.
You can run the docker client in the same system (recommended) or connect it to a remote Docker
### daemon. The Docker client and daemon communicate using a REST API, over UNIX sockets, or a
## network interface.

17.1.3 Registries
As you become more comfortable in your local environment, the best way to do this is
with [[practice](https://labs.play-with-docker.com/)](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/resources/)1032, and to be more specific - practice1033, you may want to invest in a private registry.
Private registries are highly recommended as FNB does not build any open-source images yet and
your OCEP's software should not be sent to [DockerHub](https://hub.docker.com/)1034.
17.1.4 DockerFiles
### Recipes to create a consistent, reliable, and secure instance of your application. Docker does this very
well and includes some extra magic under the hood in the way in which it utilizes "layers" to reduce the
size and speed up builds (or do the opposite if you use it wrong). Below are some examples of our
Docker image recipes that you can use as inspiration to create something that will suit your Business
Unit's needs.
17.1.4.1 OCEP Application Image (WILDFLY)
Here is an example of how to use the base images to build and deploy your application in a docker
container.
First, build your OCEP so that you get a WAR file and then place the war along with these files in the
same folder as your Dockerfile, you should then be able to build the application image.
See below Docker File content example. (This will be updated with the correct content soon).
#Pull in the centos base image shown above
FROM [docker.io/jboss/wildfly:16.0.0.Final](http://docker.io/jboss/wildfly:16.0.0.Final)1035
MAINTAINER Vuyisiile Mabuza
### RUN mkdir /opt/jboss/configuration
### RUN mkdir /opt/jboss/configuration/certs
### RUN mkdir /opt/jboss/configuration/PEPalis
#ADD wildfly-16.0.0.Final.tar.gz /opt/

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
ADD jre-8u261-linux-x64.tar.gz /opt/jboss/java
RUN ln -sf /opt/wildfly-16.0.0.Final /opt/jboss/wildfly \
&& yum -y clean all \
&& rm -rf /var/cache/yum/*
COPY --from=base --chown=dockeruser:dockeruser /opt/ /opt/
#run as root user
USER root
ARG packagename
ARG standalonexml
ARG standaloneconf
ARG dockerentrypoint
ARG environment
#JBOSS home directory
ENV JBOSS_HOME /opt/wildfly-16.0.0.Final
ENV PORT ${port}
ENV WORKDIR /opt/dockeruser
ADD fnb-life-ocep.war $JBOSS_HOME/standalone/deployments/
ADD standalone.xml $JBOSS_HOME/standalone/configuration/
ADD standalone.conf $JBOSS_HOME/bin/
ADD docker-entrypoint.sh /usr/local/bin/
# Configure the image and install the OCEP's rpm into the image, after which deploy the war from the
rpm into the respected folder and clean the cache
RUN cd $JBOSS_HOME \
&& ln -sf /opt/wildfly-16.0.0.Final /opt/wildfly \
&& cd $WORKDIR \
&& chmod +x /usr/local/bin/docker-entrypoint.sh \
&& yum -y clean all \
&& rm -rf /var/cache/yum/*
# Ensure signals are forwarded to the JVM process correctly for graceful shutdown
ENV LAUNCH_JBOSS_IN_BACKGROUND true
#expose the port you configured in your standalone.xml

EXPOSE 8080
#Entrypoint script that is started just before the container runs the CMD command

# Run as lower privalaged user to be safe
USER dockeruser
CMD ["/bin/bash", "-c", "JAVA_HOME=/opt/jboss/java/jre1.8.0_261 /opt/wildfly-16.0.0.Final/bin/
standalone.sh -b 0.0.0.0 -c standalone.xml -Djboss.server.log.dir=/opt/dockeruser/logs
-Djboss.server.base.dir=/opt/wildfly/standalone -DPLATFORM_EXTENSION_ENVIRONMENT=LOCAL
-Denvironment=LOCAL -Djdk.tls.ephemeralDHKeySize=2048"]

port=8080 -f Dockerfile --tag ocep-prepaid:1 .

PC:

Kubernetes
Installing Kubernetes with the intention of running production workloads can be quite daunting at first.
You will have to decide what environment you will be bootstrapping Kubernetes to as they will need
different configurations but the principle remains the same. Kubernetes documentation includes a lot
of detail as to how to get up and running with this. There are a number of ways that you can go about
doing this:
1. installing with [kubeadm](https://kubernetes.io/docs/setup/production-environment/tools/kubeadm/)1036
1. installing using [kubespray](https://kubernetes.io/docs/setup/production-environment/tools/kubespray/)1037
1. install using [kops](https://kubernetes.io/docs/setup/production-environment/tools/kops/)1038 (preferred for AWS)
17.1.6 Kubernetes Objects

### 17.1.6.1 Cluster
A cluster comprises a set of master/worker nodes that each run a set of pods that are allocated to
### these nodes using various criteria and take into account node-taints, availability, resource usage and
quotas, and much more. It is advisable to run at least 2 clusters for a Production environment in two
different data centers as this will provide you with high availability. These clusters can be placed
behind an API-Gateway such as HA-Proxy so that traffic can ingress into the nodes and propagate to
### the pods that will eventually serve client requests.
Clusters also have to include a control plane that includes components such as etcd, kube-schedular,
kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, flannel, etc....These components are used to make decisions
about the cluster and also detect and respond to events.
### 17.1.6.2 Node
A node in K8s terminology is a unit that runs your workload by running your pods and t[[here](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/)](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/components/#node-components)fore
applications. T[[here](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/)](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/components/#node-components) are several nodes that make up a Kubernetes cluster which may either be a virtual
or a physical machine depending on your environment. Components that a node include are the
kubelet, kube-proxy, container runtime, and addons (such as nginX ingress)
###### More information about the above can be found [[here](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/)](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/components/#node-components)1039.
### 17.1.6.3 Pod
### 17.1.6.4 Pods are what the developers will take an interest in. They are the
### smallest units of computing that you cant create and manage in K8s.
### You can think of a pod similar to the way Docker describes
containers. The form part of a deployment or deamonset and can
include init-containers and ephemeral containers or sidecars.
###### More information about the pod can be found [[here](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/)](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/components/#node-components)1040.
### 17.1.6.5 Ingress
Ingress is a method used to describe how traffic is ingested into your applications. T[[here](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/)](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/components/#node-components) are multiple
### types of ingress controllers that can be used in K8s such as Nginx, HAProxy, etc.
### 17.1.6.6 Deployment
### Deployments are how we control the instances/pods of our applications. T[[here](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/)](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/components/#node-components) are many kinds of
[deployments](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/), we choose replicaset deployments with a rolling update feature with maxUnavalable set
### to zero. This configuration will give you maximum up time even if you only have one pod running of an
application in your cluster and you force an upgrade.
###### More information about [deployments](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/)1041.

FNB Life OCEP - Local Environment Setup – 920

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
### 17.1.6.7 Service
A service is how your pod's application is reached from the outside world. Just as deployments have
### various types so too do services, there are ClusterIP, NodePort, and LoadBalancer to name a few. At
app we generally use two types:
### 1. ClusterIP
1. NodePort
### 17.1.6.7.1 ClusterIP
Kubernetes nodes all run a kube-proxuy which helps add the pods cluster-ip to the iptables, these
### clusterIP is only available within the cluster only or via kube-proxy. We then create ingress rules to
expose this service to the outside world using NginX ingress controller in our cluster that exposes a
NodePort type service that our API gateway (HAProxy) sends requests to
### 17.1.6.7.2 NodePort
NodePort services are good for [start](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tutorials/)ing out or POC purposes. A NodePort service has a range of
30000-32767. You can envision a NodePort to be a VM that has a port exposed on all nodes of your
### cluster that is reachable from outside the cluster (Exposes the Service on each Node's IP at a static
port aka. the NodePort). A ClusterIP service, to which the NodePort service routes, is automatically
### created. You'll be able to contact the NodePort service, from outside the cluster, by requesting
<NodeIP>:<NodePort>
### 17.1.7 Recommendation
It is highly recommended that you [start](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tutorials/) out with [Minikube](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/tools/install-minikube/)1042 and play around with Kubernetes. There
are many great interactive tutorials done by the Kubernetes experts. This is a good place to [start](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tutorials/)1043.
### 17.2 Wildfly Final 16.0.0.0

https://www.wildfly.org/downloads/

1. Navigate to your wildfly bin folder. C:\wildfly-16.0.0.Final\bin
1. Open standalone.conf.bat using your preferred editor (e.g Notepad++ or Notepad)
1. Add the below line into your standalone.conf.bat
set "JAVA_OPTS=%$JAVA_OPTS% -Dorg.jboss.security.ignoreHttpsHost=true
-Dsun.security.ssl.allowUnsafeRenegotiation=true

FNB Life OCEP Products – 1010

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
Client must be KYC verified.
Client must be a South African citizen with a valid SA id number.
Client age: Age of a client applying for a policy with us.
Minimum age allowed is 18.
Maximum age allowed is 74.
Policy term age: Up to what age you can have your cover active.
Call Centre and Unassisted defaulted to maximum term age (Whole life - 120 years)
Advisory uses user input with maximum term age of 120 allowed.
Do Note that for all digital channels except advisory will sell life cover at max term age at time of this
document.
###### Transactional Accounts:
Client must have any of the transactional accounts documented on the below page with FNB, with
account status of NEW_ACCOUNT or ACTIVE_ACCOUNT:
See - Life Customised DDA Accounts (see page 1016)
Payment Arrangement:
Premiums are paid monthly.
26.3.2 Cover Level Rules
All covers have a minimum entry age of 18 years.
26.3.2.1 Life Cover
Max Entry age: 74
###### Term Age: 120
Cover Escalation: Fixed Rate - 5%
Premium Escalation: 3%
Minimum cover amount: R200 000
FNB Life OCEP Products – 1011

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
Maximum cover amount: R100 000 000
##### 26.3.2.1.1 Additional Take Up Conditions
If client is pre-qualified:
Data API field PredictiveIndicator value is "Pre-Qualified".
##### Use the data API field PreQualifiedLimit value as the recommended life cover amount.
Create quote with life cover benefit only with an option to add the other benefits the client
qualifies for.
Else if client is pre-approved:
Data API field PredictiveIndicator value is "Pre-Approved".
##### Use the data API field PreApprovedLimit value as the recommended life cover amount.
Create quote with life cover benefit only with an option to add the other benefits the client
qualifies for.
Else:
##### Use the data API field LifeCover value as the recommended life cover amount.
##### Add all qualifying covers after capturing the "About Me" form UI View values.
Critical Illness and Disability should be added as Accelerated covers.
Retrenchment cover is added as a stanalone cover.
##### 26.3.2.1.2 During Cover Customisation:
If life cover is removed from quote, all accelerated covers should be converted to standalone
covers on behalf of the client.
When updating Life cover amount cannot be less than the highest accelerated cover amount.
eg. Accelerated Disability is R250 000, Accelerated Critical Illness is R200 000. Life Cover
amount cannot be less than the Accelerated Disability cover amount.
##### 26.3.2.2 Critical Illness (CI)
Max Entry age: 64
##### Term Age: 120
Cover Escalation: Fixed Rate - 5%
FNB Life OCEP Products – 1012

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
Premium Escalation: 3%
Minimum cover amount: R200 000
Maximum cover amount: R10 000 000
Data Api Field: CICover
26.3.2.2.1 During Cover Customisation:
When client selects "Maintain my full Life Cover when I claim for Critical Illness", change
current selected Critical Illness cover from Accelerated Critical Illness to Standalone Critical
Illness e.g Comprehensive CI Accelerated to Elite CI Standalone, and Accelerated Essential CI to
Standalone Essential CI.
When client selects "Pay out 100% for severity critical illness", change from Essential CI to Elite
CI (Standalone) or from Essential CI to Comprehensive CI (Accelerated CI)
If CI is accelerated when updating its cover amount, the cover amount for CI cannot be more
than Life Cover amount.
26.3.2.3 Disability
Max Entry age: 59
###### Term Age: 65
Cover Escalation: Fixed Rate - 5%
Premium Escalation: 3%
Minimum cover amount: R200 000
Maximum cover amount: R50 000 000
Data API field: DisabilityCover
26.3.2.3.1 Additional Take-up conditions:
If occupation qualifies for Permanent disability and Permanent impairment, create quote with
Accelerated Permanent disability.
If occupation qualifies for Permanent impairment only, create quote with Accelerated
Permanent impairment.
If occupation doesn't qualify for both do not offer disability at all.
FNB Life OCEP Products – 1013

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
##### 26.3.2.3.2 During Cover Customisation:
When client selects "Maintain my full Life Cover when I claim for Permanent Disability/
Impairment", change current selected cover from Accelerated Disability to Standalone Disability
or from Accelerated impairment to Standalone impairment.
Call Centre Only - When client selects "Switch to permanent impairment", change cover from
Permanent Disability to Permanent Impairment
Call Centre Only - When client selects "Switch to permanent disability", change cover from
Permanent Impairment to Permanent Disability
When client updates their occupation to an occupation that doesn't qualify for permanent
disability but qualifies for impairment, change cover to permanent impairment.
Unassisted Only - When client updates their occupation to an occupation that qualify for
permanent disability but have impairment cover, change cover to permanent disability.
When client updates their occupation to an occupation that doesn't qualify for qualify for both
permanent disability and permanent impairment, remove cover disability.
If CI is accelerated when updating its cover amount, the cover amount for CI cannot be more
##### than Life Cover amount.
##### 26.3.2.4 Retrenchment
Max Entry age: 59
###### Term Age: 65
Cover Escalation: By Index, Consumer Price Index (CPI)
Premium Escalation: Reviewed annually.
Minimum cover amount: R2000 pm
Maximum cover amount: R50 000 pm
Employment status: Contract work / Formally Employed
##### 26.3.2.4.1 During Cover Customisation:
### Retrenchment cannot be the only cover on the quote. There should always be at least one of
##### these covers paired with retrenchment: Life Cover, Perment Disability/Impairment, Critical
Illness
### Retrenchment cover amount x 12 months cannot be more than R600 000
### Retrenchment cover amount x 12 months cannot be more than the total amount of other
##### standalone covers.
Chosen Cover < Minimum retrenchment cover:
FNB Life OCEP Products – 1014

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
Use minimum cover amount as retrenchment cover amount.
Chosen Cover > Max cover:
Use maximum cover amount as retrenchment cover amount.
Pre-approved Cover < Chosen Cover and Referral Threshold < Chosen Cover:
Require employment information to be captured and trigger the retrenchment referral screen.
Pre-approved Cover < Referral Threshold < Chosen Cover:
Require employment information to be captured and Income validation required.
Referral Threshold < Chosen Cover < Pre-Approved Cover:
Income validation required.
Pre-approved Cover < Chosen Cover < Referral Threshold:
Require employment information to be captured.
Chosen Cover > Pre-Approved Cover and Chosen Cover == Referral Threshold:
Require employment information to be captured.
Chosen Cover > Referral Threshold and Chosen Cover == Pre-Approved Cover:
Income validation required.
Chosen Cover < Pre-Approved Cover and Chosen Cover < Referral Threshold:
Income validation is not required.
Employment information is not required.

##### 33.1.1.2.4 Service Calls
##### 33.1.1.2.4.1 Interface Usage
All service calls MUST be done via the interface and the implementation provided to do so. This
interface will be available under the service layer.
An alternative implementation MAY be requested and MUST be evaluated and approved before
use.
##### 33.1.1.2.4.2 Logging
##### Service call request and response strings MUST be logged (see [Logging Standards](https://file+.vscode-resource.vscode-cdn.net/c%3A/Users/F5338069/OneDrive%20-%20FRG/Desktop/standards/Life_OCEP_Technical_Standards.md#11-logging-standards)1160 for
format).
##### If an alternative implementation has been approved, a logical way to bind request and response
##### logs to each other MUST also be provided.
##### 33.1.1.2.4.3 Data Format
The use of Gson (JSON) is the required format for service calls.
The use of XML Requests and Response's for services MAY be declined due to no longer using
PEP-v2.
##### 33.1.1.2.4.4 Service Construction
Pre-population of a service is discouraged. A model to build the service SHOULD be used
instead - that way when a service call needs to be made with the same YAML, a service update
would not be required.
##### 33.1.1.2.4.5 Version Tracking
All updates to YAMLs MUST be tracked by version for service files.
Example: If you are using dataAPI and there's a minor enhancement to the YAML, increase
##### the version on our end either to match that of the new schema version, or in worst case (where
##### there's no version for the API) increase it by 1.
##### 33.1.1.2.4.6 Generic JsonType Prohibition
No service call is allowed to use a generic JsonType by default.
Generic JsonType s MUST NOT be used unless there is absolutely no other way to solve the
problem.
Even in the worst case, push for an API re-design first - generic types where the name is resolved
##### at runtime cause problems down the line if there are changes on a service provider.

#### 33.1.1.2.6.3 UIID Naming
```
All UIIDs MUST be named by function. Looking at a UIID SHOULD clearly specify what the screen or
action does.
```
#### UIID Format (BNF-style grammar):
```
<uiid> ::= <prefix> "." <component> "." <channel> "."
<layer> "." [feature] "." <action> "." <name> "." <type>
<prefix> ::= "ui.life" | "model.life"
<component> ::= "lc" | "clp" | <product-acronym>
<channel> ::= "app" | "cc" | "aop"
<layer> ::= "views" | "controllers" | "models"
[feature] ::= <lowercase-string> (e.g.
"beneficiary", "payments")
<action / flow / work item> ::= <lowercase-string> (e.g. "add",
"maintain", "delete" ...)
<name> ::= <lowercase-string> (e.g.
"addbeneficiary")
<type> ::= "view" | "form.controller" | "controller"
```

33.1.1.2.7 OCEP MVC Standard
33.1.1.2.7.1 Views
```
All UI elements MUST use symbols.size() ordering. The only exception is string literal
ordering (e.g. "0" ), used only where certain orders need to be maintained.
A view MUST only be linked to 1 model.
A view SHOULD ideally have 1 or 2 controllers: one for entry and one for form validations.
Dynamic elements MUST be data-oriented - value and errors SHOULD come from cache.
The use of Cerebro MUST NOT be used in new code. Developers MUST use the async API
instead.
```
33.1.1.2.7.2 Errors
```
Errors MUST be handled by cache and placed into cache as they happen, with the key of the
```
symbol throwing the error.
```
Errors SHOULD be cleared on a model update of that component, unless there is a documented
```
business reason not to.
1161. http://ui.life.lc.cc

```

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
Errors that cannot be displayed on a component MUST be placed in either a paragraph or as part
of a specific error screen.
Errors SHOULD be cleared on the entry of a controller and re-added when validation fails.
##### 33.1.1.2.7.3 Controller Logic
Any entry into an application MUST be via a controller that will then route to the appropriate
view.
All entry controllers MUST be in their own package indicating that it is an entry into the
application.
##### 33.1.1.2.7.4 Models
Models MUST extend LifeModel .
The initiatedSymbol MUST be obtained by using the getInitiatedSymbol method.
Developers MUST use the device country and the skin from
the PlatformExtensionFramework when building Symbols.

#### 33.1.1.2.8 OCEP Symbol Creation
#### 33.1.1.2.8.1 Always Include the Library Reference
```
When creating a symbol, the SymbolFactory class reference MUST always be included. This
```
makes it explicit which library the symbol is coming from.
```
Allowed:
SymbolFactory.addViewSwitcher("0.view.switcher", sc.getHeader().getKey(),
SymbolColour.PAPER, "0")
.withLeftColour(SymbolColour.PRIMARY, SymbolColour.PRIMARY,
SymbolColour.PAPER)
.withRightColour(SymbolColour.PAPER, SymbolColour.PRIMARY,
SymbolColour.PRIMARY)
.withText("Active policies", "Inactive policies")
.withSelectedAs(true, false)
.withUIIDs("", "ui.life.phone.insurance.landing.inactive.policies.view.mm")
.withBgColour(SymbolColour.PAPER)
.addToContainer(sc.getHeader());
```
Not Allowed:
```

#### 33.1.1.2.8.2 No Separate Methods for Creating Views
##### The Platform Extension Framework already exposes builders for items. Developers MUST NOT extract
#### symbol creation into separate methods.
```
Allowed - inline symbol creation:
// Spacer above content
SymbolFactory.addSpacer(sc.getKey() + ".spacer.1", sc.getKey(), SymbolColour.GLASS,
"" + order++)
.withHeight(5)
.addToContainer(sc.getBody());
// Illustration image
SymbolFactory.addImage("no.quotes.error", sc.getBody().getKey(), "" + order++)
.withAlignment(Alignment.CENTER)
.withImage("document.magnify.reject.illustration")
.addToContainer(sc.getBody());
// Spacer between image and text

"" + order++)
.withHeight(4)
.addToContainer(sc.getBody());

.withText("There are no active policies. Please add a policy")
.withAlignment(Alignment.CENTER)
.withStyle(SymbolColour.INK)
.addToContainer(sc.getBody());

buildBeneficiaryView(cache);

33.1.1.2.8.4 No var Keyword
All types MUST be explicitly stated. The var keyword MUST NOT be used.
Allowed:
```
for (Item item : itemList) { ... }
Product myProductHere = new Product();
Not Allowed:
for (var item : itemList) { ... }
```
var myProductHere = new Product();
33.1.1.2.8.5 APP and AOP Separation
The following decision flowchart governs how code is shared (or not) between APP and AOP:
Is this UI-layer code (views, controllers, models)?
```
├── YES → MUST be in separate packages for APP and AOP. No sharing.
└── NO → Is this business-layer logic?
├── YES → Is the code identical for both APP and AOP?
│ ├── YES → Place under the `shared` package.
│ │ ├── MUST provide APP/AOP selection at minimum.
│ │ ├── MUST NOT change the function signature.
│ │ └── MUST NOT change the function execution.
│ └── NO → Does the difference affect the function signature?
│ ├── YES → Create a NEW businessLayerService under
│ │ the specific channel's implementation.
│ └── NO → Is it a minor logic branch for one channel?
│ ├── YES → MAY check for the channel directly
│ │ and navigate accordingly.
│ └── NO → Create separate implementations.
└── NO → Evaluate on a case-by-case basis.
```
Rules summary:
You MUST NOT use the same code for both APP and AOP interchangeably. There MUST be two
separate packages for APP and AoP as they are separate concerns.
You MAY use the same businessLayer logic between APP and AOP, given that the code
```
is closed for modification once the dev is done.
#### 1. OCEP – 1144

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
"Closed for modification" means: no changes to the function signature AND no changes to
the function's execution logic. Bug fixes that do not alter the contract are permitted.
Any code in the business layer that is shared between APP and AOP MUST go under
the shared package, and MUST have the option to select APP/AOP at the bare minimum for
execution.
If the requesting channel requires a different type of response not needed on the other
application, a new businessLayerService MUST be created under the specific
implementation.
If there's a slight logic difference affecting only one channel, you MAY check for the channel
directly and navigate accordingly.
##### 33.1.1.2.9 PlatformExtension XML Files
Platform extension XML files MUST be under:
ocep-application/resources/platform-extension/ui/**
##### 33.1.1.2.9.1 Grouping Options
Platform extension XML files MAY be grouped by:
a. Screen
One XML file equals one screen. This XML file will hold:
The screen (UI) itself
The controller
The model
b. Feature
One XML file holds a full feature or flow. This file will be sorted from controller to view, all in one file.
Example - Add Payments flow:
getPaymentInfoController PaymentInfoView paymentValidationFormController
getOtherPaymentInfoController getOtherPaymentInfoView otherPaymentValidationFormController
Ordering Rule
The XML file MUST be sorted top to bottom in chronological order - meaning if A points to B, then B
MUST be declared under A.
##### 1. OCEP – 1145

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
##### 33.1.1.2.10 Logging Standards
##### 33.1.1.2.10.1 Logger
All logging MUST use SLF4J as the logging facade.
Logback is the recommended implementation.
Developers MUST NOT use System.out.println or System.err.println for logging.
##### 33.1.1.2.11 Error Handling Strategy
##### 33.1.1.2.11.1 UI-Layer Errors
##### See OCEP MVC Standard - Errors1165 for UI error handling via cache.
##### 33.1.1.2.11.2 Service-Layer Errors
All service call exceptions MUST be caught and handled gracefully. The application MUST NOT
expose stack traces to the user.
##### Service call failures MUST be logged at ERROR level with the correlation ID, request payload
##### summary, and exception message.
##### 33.1.1.2.11.3 Unhandled Exceptions
A global exception handler MUST be in place to catch any unhandled exceptions.
Unhandled exceptions MUST be logged at ERROR level and MUST result in a generic error
##### screen for the user.
##### 33.1.1.2.12 Security Standards
##### 33.1.1.2.12.1 Input Validation
All user input MUST be validated on the server side, regardless of client-side validation.
Validation errors MUST be returned to the UI via the cache-based error mechanism.
##### 33.1.1.2.12.2 Data in Transit
All communication between OCEP and backend services MUST use HTTPS/TLS.
HTTP (non-TLS) endpoints MUST NOT be used in any environment including development.

##### 33.1.1.2.13 Performance Guidelines
##### 33.1.1.2.13.1 Caching Strategy
Frequently accessed, rarely changing data SHOULD be cached to reduce service call overhead.
Cache entries MUST have a defined TTL (time-to-live) appropriate to the data's volatility.
Cache invalidation MUST be handled explicitly - do not rely on TTL alone for data that can
##### change mid-session.
##### 33.1.1.2.13.2 Timeouts
All service calls MUST have a configured timeout.
Recommended defaults:
Connection timeout: 5 seconds
Read timeout: 20 seconds
Timeout values SHOULD be configurable per service and MUST NOT be hardcoded.
##### 33.1.1.2.14 Git & Branching Strategy
##### 33.1.1.2.14.1 Branch Naming
Branches MUST follow this naming convention:
```
<initials>-<type>-<short-description>
```
Type Usage
feature New feature development
bugfix Bug fixes
Release Release preparation
Example: rc- feature-add-beneficiary
##### 33.1.1.2.14.2 Onboarding
New developers MUST read this document as part of their onboarding.
A walkthrough session with a senior developer SHOULD be conducted.

### 33.1.1.3 Documentation
### 33.1.1.3.1 CodeDocumentation
All code needs to have a purpose. code without purpose is considered dead code and adds to
### technical debt for removal thereof at a later point.
The idea behind code documentation is to ensure that other developers know what's actually going on
in the code and why things are happening the way they are.
Code needs to be self documenting in a way that reading the code makes you understand 90% of
what's actually going on. The core idea is to have propper naming for functions within the business
layer to communicate to the next developer what's going on.
### 33.1.1.3.2 Confluence Documentation
Code, flows and entrypoints SHOULD be documented on confluence. This means that a new developer
will be able to read one simple document and fully understand everything of a project. This will
eliminate the case of FRS hunting to try and figure out what happend on what microservice and why.
This documentation should ideally be like a well written flow chart. Preferably similar to that which the
SA's would produce. the idea would be to understand core concepts and how they work in regards to
### certain screens. business rules as well as what happens technically at what stage.
NOTE that this is not a code dump! We do not want to see code dumped here that's what GIT and the
source code is for. this should only be the functionality of a microservice or service that you worked
on.
### any dev that has some free time should go back to the code they have written and document the
### usage of the code back into confluence for future devs to understand.
This document may hold all of the FRS's over the years to be able to reference, but they should not be
### the source of truth. the source of truth should be this document itself. stating what the core logic is,
what service calls we are making at which points and what the expected business result is.
NOTE this documentation may be out of date from time to time, but the idea is to get other devs 90%
onboard with a project and understanding that project. the other 10% the code will assist the dev with.

### 33.1.4 Interactions Metadata
### 33.1.4.1 Reason for interactions:
Interactions data is there to get insights into what is happening where when we are making use of an
app.
The idea is that these interactions should be more than enough data to report on and know what is
happening when on the app.
We would be able to see is a certain controller fails or passes ect. Interactions are only available on
OCEP Views.
The following assumes that you are running with a FNBLifePlatformExtensionFramework that
supports Redis.
Please note running the application with redis will need you to setup a redis server to connect to when
you are testing cache.
You would have to run the two following applications for the application to work:
→ Redis Server
→ MY APP
(ensure it has the following dependency in the pom)
→FNBLifePlatformExtensionFramework (ensure this version has the following features)
→ Cache Abstractions

33.1.6.1 0 - Understanding OCEP Architecture
Full flow:
### USER → Core OCEP → PEP → HA → MS
External:
### USER → Core OCEP → PEP
###### Internal:
HA → MS
33.1.6.1.1
###### Request Responses of OCEP.
###### To be brief within this section I will not mention the use of HAProxy but simply the ocep itself. the
eg
### User→ Core OCEP → PEP -> HAProxy → OCEP_MS_1(where we process the request)→ HaProxy →
PEP → Core OCEP → User
will be simplified to only talk to
OCEP_MS_1 where this is a example microservice.
all requests follow the path as mentioned but we will discuss that below this section
OCEP is a framework that allows us to create front end applications from the back end.
###### We will specify what we want someone to see on the screen and the specific OCEP platform eg IOS
FNB App (on V60 for example) will then render it accordingly.
given a response or what a screen will look like, we will need a way to know what a customer did, from
what device and possibly if they where assisted or not.
###### There's tons of this information and it all comes in through a form field on OCEP.
### 1. OCEP – 1160

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
OCEP in itself is stateless for the most part, but we as the OCEP Partner need to keep the state of a
customer. We have the request sessionId that we can use for this.
a sesionID is something that allows the customer to be identified within the same session. Please
note that the sessionId can change due to something called "sesisonResume" where long lived
sessions are then "reset" to be able to continue. for this reason the latest code will not make use of
sessionId but rather a customer's deviceId.
We as FNBLife OCEP have 2 ways of caching.
1. OCEP Cache
This is cache that sits in the sessionContext, it is basically a hash map that works against the
core ocep framework, this is a older version of cache that we try and avoid.
1. Redis Cache
this is cache that sits within a redis data base. this cache is either built with the request
sessionId or possibly the deviceId depending on when this micro service has been created, most
should sit against the device Id
OCEP Responses will be logged something like this, we can go over what everything means within
later documentation of this getting started list

version for easier demonstration of the fields

the path here is the registered "route" for the lack of a better word of what to do. this is called a
uiid

###### As you can see you have access to tons of information about a client when a single request it made.
each request is a request where the customer does something.
a way to think of this is almost a "when a customer clicks"
so when customer clicks on a button the microservice will process that request and will ultimately
return a view, a updated to a view or redirect response to the customer.
we send XML as a response and Core OCEP translates it to the correct symbol (display) on the front
end.
1. OCEP – 1162

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
here's some examples of this
When the customer clicks on a dropdown we will process that request and then show a update to the
view adding the popup to the screen.
When the customer clicks on a 'x' button to close a popup we will process that request and then show
a update to the view removing the popup from the screen.
When the customer clicks on the "Continue" button our OCEP will navigate you to a new screen for
example from covers to payments
When the customer clicks the "Continue" button on sorry to see you go we will pick up via a controller,
this controller will redirect the customer to another ocep
##### 33.1.6.1.2 HA Proxy and routing
HA Proxy or high availability proxy is a tool that allows us to spread the load between two OCEP nodes
effectively.
the way HAProxy works is that it has rules and routing rules as well as backends.
the file can be found at: /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg
to register a path you do the following:
acl ALIS_SERVICING_URL path_reg \/fnb-life-yethu\/(UI|DATA)\/(ui|
model).life.insurance.vcl.alis.servicing.*
this tells HAProxy to register a path using regex
we register a backend the following way:
backend alis_servicing
balance roundrobin
cookie platform_extension_sessionid prefix nocache
server lfe-rbocintap01 127.0.0.1:8088 ssl verify required ca-file /etc/ssl/certs/ca-bundle.crt inter
##### 2000 cookie [lfe-rbocintap01.fnb.co.za](http://lfe-rbocintap01.fnb.co.za)1169check
this basically tells HAProxy how to route the traffic
we created a "alis-servicing" backend and we are keeping a cookie for it. the server where we send the
information to is ssl verified by the path.
once we have the route definition and we have the backend we need to be able to tell it where it should
go :
use_backend alis_servicing if ALIS_SERVICING_URL
##### 1169. http://[lfe-rbocintap01.fnb.co.za](http://lfe-rbocintap01.fnb.co.za)
##### 1. OCEP – 1163

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
this tells us that if we match the regex pattern of "ALIS_SERVICING_URL" that we should use the
backend "alist_servicing"
use backend will be read top to bottom and will match on the first occurrence it finds
here's a example :
[http://localhost:8080/fnb-life-yethu/UI/ui.life.insurance.vcl.alis.servicing.start](http://localhost:8080/fnb-life-yethu/UI/ui.life.insurance.vcl.alis.servicing.start)
will route to [http://127.0.0.1:8088/fnb-life-yethu/UI/ui.life.insurance.vcl.alis.servicing.start](http://localhost:8080/fnb-life-yethu/UI/ui.life.insurance.vcl.alis.servicing.start)1170.
if there where more servers in the list for a backend HAProxy will choose one from the list using the
round robin selection method

you can set the password using the command like this:
"CONFIG SET requirepass passwordgoeshere" (note this will set the password to be
"passwordgoeshere")
you can test any config changes please make use of redis-cli. you can view the common commands
for redis
a simple auth check would look like this:
1. start the cli
1. set the config (this does not persist)
1. authenticate against the server
1. try and see what keys are currently set

### 33.5 POCs
### 33.5.1 Life OCEP Distributed Caching POC
### 33.5.1.1 BRS
Name Ruben Coetzer
### Date 2025-03-10
Business Requirement Specification for React
### 1. Introduction
This document outlines the business requirements for a technical modification that allows system
### stability. The modification is straightforward, with the primary functionality of caching a user’s session
on FNB Life microservices
### 1. Purpose
The purpose of the app is to give users the current time based on their device’s local time zone. It will
### be useful for people who want to quickly check the time without navigating to the system clock or
other apps
The purpose of the technical change is to allow a user’s state to be stored outside of a physical
### application, allowing for dynamic node balancing and ensuring that we can make use of the async
### service for pushing screens to the user for a given public session keeping all information that has been
provided.
### 1. Scope
The upgrade will:
Cover the VCL app
### 1. Objectives
### Setting VCL to make use of cache object from the DB
### 33.5.1.2 FRS
Functional Requirements Specification Caching
### 1. OCEP – 2298

| Author: | Ruben Coetzer |
| --- | --- |
| Date | 2025-03-10 |
FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
Author: Ruben Coetzer
Date 2025-03-10
1. Introduction
The purpose of this document is to define the functional requirements for implementing a Database
Caching System for the FNB Life microservices. The goal is to reduce server load and enhance the
performance of the system by caching allowing for async calls and keeping data for those calls. This
cache will store a customer’s session.
1. Objectives
Allow for the use of async service calls allowing to keep all data
Allow for the nodes to be balanced, spun up and down without problems
1. Scope
This caching system will be implemented on FNB Life microservices. The system will cache the
customer’s session and allow a customer to retrieve their session on a subsequent request.
1. Functional Requirements
4.1. Cache Layer
The caching system will interact with the VCL application.
Save Cache
The system will save the user’s session object to cache in JSON format
Retrieve Cache
The system will retrieve the user’s session from cache in JSON format
Cache Miss Handling
If data is not found in the cache (cache miss), the system will throw a Cache Expiration
Cache Timeout
The system will only keep cache active for 10 mins, after that the system will kick out the cache
Cache Logging
The system shall have logs enabled for debug purposes
Cache has to be available to one or more nodes.
The cache system should make use of Redis for caching and be easy to use by extending
existing functionality
1. Non-Functional Requirements
5.1. Performance
1. OCEP – 2299

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
The cache system should return cached data in sub-millisecond time for cache hits.
The cache should be capable of handling thousands of concurrent requests efficiently.
5.4. Security
Access to the cache should be secured using appropriate mechanisms, such as encryption and
authentication.
1. Constraints
The system may have a memory limit for the cache storage, depending on the selected
backend (e.g., Redis or Memcached).
1. Glossary
Cache: A temporary storage area for frequently accessed data.
Cache Hit: When data is found in the cache.
Cache Miss: When data is not found in the cache, triggering a database query.
Eviction: The process of removing old or least-used data from the cache to make room for new
data.
### 33.5.1.3 OCEP Distributed Caching Architecture
As the OCEP team we are making a push to use caching to improve our systems performance,
reliability and to scale technically. For this to be achieved we need to familiarize ourselves with the
concept of External/Distributed Caching.
### 33.5.1.3.1 What is Distributed caching?
### Distributed caching is the practice of storing caching data across multiple machines or servers rather
than keeping the data locally within a single server or application instance. This allows for multiple
application instances to access a common, centralized store of cache data.
1. OCEP – 2300

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
##### 33.5.1.3.2 What technologies do we use for Distributed Caching?
Generally, in order to add a caching layer to applications or services an in-memory database is use
##### such as Redis, Memcached, Hazelcast to name a few. The reason why an in-memory database is used
instead of a normal database such as Postgres or MongoDB is purely due to speed of reading and
##### writing data. To put this into perspective we need to look at 2 things Latency (time per operation) and
##### throughput (operations per second).
For example:
PostgresSQL (Disk-based)
Ave latency: 1-10 milliseconds per query
Ave throughput: 1000-10 000 queries per second
Redis (In-memory/RAM)
Ave latency: less than 1 millisecond ranging between 0.1-0.3 milliseconds
Throughput: 100 000 - 1 000 000 operations per second.
Note these are estimates and can vary between systems depending on hardware network speed etc...
##### 1. OCEP – 2301

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
##### 33.5.1.3.3 Getting started with v53.1
In order to integrate our distributed caching methodology, Upgrade all of our applications to Platform
Extension Framework v53.1. This new version provides developers with all the necessary tools read
##### and write to Redis effortlessly. v53.1 is an extension of the original v53 version and adds features to
##### automatically read and write our session cache. By extending the platform extension we can ensure
##### the following:
All applications will follow the same standards when reading and writing to Redis
Implementation remains the same across all applications
Reading and writing to Redis is automatic
##### 33.5.1.3.3.1 Design
Below is the UML showing the basic design of the controller, model, redirect and view. Notice that
##### there are new methods that will need to be implemented namely: initiateCache,
processMessageWithCache and processInteractionData.
##### 33.5.1.3.3.2 Implementation
Prerequisites:
###### JDK 17 needs to be installed on your machine and your application must use JDK 17 (All
##### applications were moved to Java 17 in 2024)
Pull the [FnbLifePlatformExtension](https://git.fnb.co.za/fnb-insurance/fnb-life-ocep/app/fnblifeplatformextension)1216 repo from gitlab onto your local machine:
Once pulled, Switch to branch V53.1
##### run: mvn clean install
Make sure the project builds successfully
##### 33.5.1.3.3.3 Step 1 - Upgrade to v53.1 & add FNBLifePlatformExtension dependency to
##### application:
Firstly, we need to remove any other platform extension framework (PEF) dependency from our
##### application so that we can use [FnbLifePlatformExtension](https://git.fnb.co.za/fnb-insurance/fnb-life-ocep/app/fnblifeplatformextension) instead. Generally, the dependency we need
##### to remove is "commons-ocep-app" from the "common-artifacts" library, but this depends on whether
##### the application uses the common-artifacts library or houses the platform extension framework within
##### the application.
##### 1216.[ https://git.fnb.co.za/fnb-insurance/fnb-life-ocep/app/fnblifeplatformextension](https://git.fnb.co.za/fnb-insurance/fnb-life-ocep/app/fnblifeplatformextension)
##### 1. OCEP – 2302

<version>7.0</version>

33.5.1.3.3.4 Step 2 - Move project dependencies from javax namespace to jakarta
The change from javax to jakarta refers to the rebranding and renaming of java EE to jakarta EE. This
```
is due Oracle transferring the rights to the java EE to the Eclipse foundation in 2017. Unfortunately,
with this transfer Oracle still retained ownership of the javax trademark namespace giving birth to the
Jakarta namespace from the eclipse foundation. As Life OCEP we are also impacted by this and as a
requirement of PFE v53 & java 17 we need to rename all of our namespaces from javax to jakarta.
For Example:
##### javax.servlet → jakarta.servlet
##### javax.persistance → jakarta.persistance
etc...
```
To do this change our applications we need to do the following:

##### 33.5.1.3.4 Redis Infrastructure
##### 33.5.1.3.4.1 What is Redis?
Redis (Remote Dictionary Server) is an in-memory key-value store known for its speed and flexibility.
it is often used for caching, real-time analytics, message brokering, and session storage.
##### 33.5.1.3.4.2 What is an in-memory store?
In-memory means that data is stored on the host’s RAM (Random Access Memory) and not on disk.
Reading and writing from the RAM is much faster than performing disk operations. This allows in-
memory stores, such as Redis, to perform millions of requests per second.
##### 1. OCEP – 2308

FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
The in-memory storage model comes with its disadvantages. RAM is a lot more expensive than disk
storage and therefore not cost-effective for large data sets. Simply put, your data set is limited by the
memory allocated for the Redis process.
##### 33.5.1.3.4.3 What is a key-value store?
Key-value stores treat the data as a single collection. Each record in the collection is a pair—a key and
a value associated with it. Keys must be unique as they are used to retrieve values.
The data types and allowed structures for keys and values are implementation specific. For keys,
Redis allows you to use binary safe strings up to 512 MB. For values, you can choose from a wider
range of data structures. Among the supported types are strings, lists, sets, maps, and streams.
A disadvantage of using a key-value store, such as Redis, is that there’s no query language.
Additionally, Redis doesn’t natively support secondary indexes. This limits your data access flexibility.
If you need an access path to the data different from the primary key, you have to build and maintain
your own indexes, storing them in the already limited memory.
##### 33.5.1.3.4.4 Infrastructure
Below is a diagram that briefly explains Redis in our infrastructure:
Our HAproxy server hosts Redis Database
Node 1 & 2 host App, Online, AOP and Microservices
Each application either hosted on Wildfly or Microservice reads and writes to the Redis
database.
##### 1. OCEP – 2309

| Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- |
| Speed accessing data from an in-memory database is
quicker then constantly querying a DB or Service | Complex implementation in the beginning,
requires code refactoring |
| Remove sticky session allowing our HAProxy to distribute
load efficiently to each node | Ongoing management of distributed cache |
| Flexibility to scale cache to more nodes | Added learning curve |
| High system availability and fault tolerance | Difficult to debug |
| Less database load down stream | Requires more reliance on monitoring tools
because sessions are not restricted to 1
server
When sticky sessions are removed |
| Horizontal scalability can be added as applications grow and
new are added | Increased need for regression testing |
FNB Life OCEP – FNB Life - OCEP Home
By setting up Redis in this way we achieve:
Cache that is outside of our application instance meaning that our user sessions can run on
either server if one is overloaded without impacting the user.
Cache is common between all applications = 1 source of truth
##### If coupled with Kubernetes & containerization if an application dies or fails a new Instance can
##### be spawned without affecting the user session. Similarly, in this setup if an application fails on
##### node 1 traffic can be moved from node 1 to node 2 without session interruption handled by the
HAProxy.
